objective_for_doctor: Evaluate and manage a patient presenting with epigastric discomfort and cramping pain.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

“I’ve had epigastric discomfort with cramping pain for about two hours, and it feels similar to past episodes that usually happen after I eat. I’ve also unintentionally lost weight because I’ve been avoiding meals to prevent the pain.”
Thank you for that information. To help assess for potential complications, have you noticed any black, tarry stools, vomiting blood, or coffee-ground material recently?
“No, I haven’t noticed black tarry stools, vomiting blood, or anything like coffee-ground material. I also haven’t had nausea or any change in my bowel habits.”
To help narrow this down, how long after you begin eating does the pain typically start?
“It usually starts fairly soon after I begin eating—within about 15 to 30 minutes—and then the discomfort and cramping can last for a bit after.”
How old are you, and do you have any history of smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or known cardiovascular disease?
“I’m 38 years old, and I do smoke; I don’t have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or any known cardiovascular disease.”
Do you regularly take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen, or aspirin?
“I don’t take any regular NSAIDs for it, but for my chronic knee pain I use over-the-counter painkillers occasionally—usually around-the-day as needed.”
Does the pain radiate to your back or right shoulder, or does it remain localized to the center of your upper abdomen?
“It stays mostly in the center of my upper abdomen and doesn’t really radiate to my back or right shoulder. It’s just epigastric discomfort with cramping that comes on shortly after I start eating.”
Does taking antacids or acid-reducing medications (like omeprazole or famotidine) provide any noticeable relief to the discomfort?
“I haven’t tried antacids or acid-reducing medications yet, so I can’t say whether they help. I’ve just been avoiding meals because the pain tends to come on after I start eating.”
[DDX] Gastric ulcer, Chronic gastritis, Duodenal ulcer, Functional dyspepsia, Biliary colic
